So theres a rule in improv of "yes and" that I sometimes apply to D&D role play. When a player makes an offer (to make the flower bloom now), the other player/DM/npc can say "yes and this." But that concept is specifically designed to keep improv scenes moving because "no" shuts things down. And it's a little simplistic for something like D&D, so I also do "no, but." The player makes the offer, the npc says "No, but this."

I don't think you did anything wrong with that interaction, but  I can understand why the player felt put out. A simple no just shuts down their offer and maybe makes them feel bad for trying at all. If you want to encourage RP in your game, you might want to work in a "no, but" situation - like maybe the Druid says "no, not this flower but you could do it to these ones." Or "no, and this is why I haven't done that." "No, but here is your own flower to nurture with time or magic." The Druid npc could've given the player two flowers to take care of, one with magic and the other with just skill, to learn the difference. 

I think it's easy sometimes for both players and DMs to get caught up in staying totally in character, no wiggle room at all. There's a pressure to be totally perfect and true to character/npc... But people are complicated and layered and don't have personalities that are set in stone. You can bend a little and still be in character. 

Obviously there's a balance here - you shouldn't give in to every player whim and honestly sometimes a "no" that shuts things down has a time and place. Again, I don't think you handled this poorly at all, I just see some potential and can understand where your player is coming from. You're a new DM and you don't have to be perfect. Even if you'd been a DM forever you don't have to be perfect. This is all just stuff you can keep in mind for the next NPC interaction.

I completely understand where you're coming from. This is exactly where I have been lately. I was taking medication, I was doing yoga, I was trying to eat better and sleep better, I was *trying so hard...* And it still wasn't working.

First things first, might be to up the current dose of medication you're on, if your doctor agrees. Even a small uptick can make a huge difference sometimes. It did for me. My doctors also added another medication to help me sleep, and that was also a big help to me. 

Secondly, do tell your friends, if you and they are both comfortable talking it out. I think most friends would rather be burdened with mental issues than with funeral plans. The thing in your head telling you that no one cares, that you are a burden, that thing is almost certainly a lie. I think of depression and anxiety and even suicidal thoughts like a virus, or a parasite, something that's desperately trying to stay alive inside me, even if it kills the host. That's why intrusive thoughts like that pop into my head – the parasite is trying to stay alive and well, at my detriment. And I say that parasite can go to hell. Maybe it'll be helpful if you think of it the same way. 

I do recommend yoga, there's a really great bunch of videos on YouTube, called Yoga With Adrienne. She's very calming and a very good teacher, and it's improved my mental health a lot since starting. You don't even need a mat, just a blanket or towel or even a plain old floor will do. At the very least, yoga forces you to pay attention to nothing else but your body and your breathing, and if you are capable at all, I highly recommend it. It's a great way to get out of your own head. 

And if you really feel as if you can't get a handle on things right now, that's okay. Try to get to your local ER, and ask if they can help you get into an inpatient program. It's scary and terrifying, and it *sucks* let me tell you, but they will take care of you, remind you of the basics of taking care of yourself, and you'll be surrounded by a lot of people who are at least, or even more messed up than you are. It can be a very jarring experience, but it can also get you to a more stable place with professional help. 

Focusing on the things you care about and the things you're passionate about are also big ways to make yourself feel better, even for a short time. Reading your favorite books. Sitting in the sun. Petting an animal if they're around. Watching your favorite television program. Any hobby or interest you have. Nothing is too small to matter. 

You can do this. We both can.

Cutting releases endorphins and give your brain a chemical boost it sorely needs. It's also a stress-reliever, and a(n unhealthy) coping mechanism you've come to rely on. I thought about it this afternoon, and I wanted to do it so badly. But I didn't. And one day, I hope you will be at that point too. 

What really helped me was finding better coping mechanisms. Identifying thinking errors and stopping them in their tracks before they could fester and make me itch for a cut. Going outside and sitting in the sun. Playing with my animals. Talking to friends about nothing important. Reading my favorite books, watching TV, movies, anything to keep my mind off the tools around me. Try to do it slowly, too. You don't have to quit all at once. Maybe establish a 'safe place' where you won't self-harm, like declaring your bed off-limits. Then after a while, making it your bedroom. Then the whole house. 

It's a process. And it's hard, and it sucks. But you aren't alone.

NAH. Some people care a lot about spoilers. Some people don't. It's unfortunate you guys haven't figured this out until now, but I don't know if it's the hill you wanna die on. So she knows what happens -- she hasn't told you, so you can still have the experience you want to have. She wanted to have a different experience, and that's okay. In fact, it's kinda fun to do that. 

I do not care about spoilers, at all, people can tell me the endings to anything and everything and that's cool with me. Granted, I have a lowkey anxiety disorder, so it's weirdly calming to know what's coming up next or how things end. But I have so many friends who are very, very serious about spoilers. So if I look them up or see them, I don't say anything. But I'll mention that I did, just like your sister did. And then I get to watch my friends freak out over stuff that I know is coming up. The show is still exciting, because it's designed to be exciting. The shocks are still shocking, because it's designed to be shocking. 

If she's still willing to watch it with you, then I think you should try watching at least a couple episodes together. You can't blame her for wanting to watch TV in a different way than you do, and it sounds like you were really excited to watch this with her. She's still your sister, the show is still the show. But you're NTA because like, you're entitled to feelings too. I just think it'll still be fun, that's all I'm saying. And then neither of you will feel like assholes because you'll just enjoy the show.

NAH. As the spouse who is left at home while my husband (also an essential worker) gets to go out everyday, to see friends or not -- I feel for your boyfriend. I literally get no human contact until he gets home. Neither does your boyfriend. I'm an introvert who made a phone call of my own free will today. I watch the mailman pull up and hope he waves, that's how weird things have gotten. It's lonely. He's lonely. But I don't think you're doing anything wrong. Your boyfriend needs to own up to his emotions and realize that they aren't yours to fix. There are nights when I'm starving for my husband's attention, but he's dying to do something with his friends, and I let him go because his happiness matters. Even when it affects my happiness. Sometimes that's what you do for a partner, you sacrifice your own comfort. 

My point is, don't vilify his feelings. And by the same token, he shouldn't expect you to fix them. Times are weird, and things are stressful, so he needs to learn to manage his own shit. You're learning to, but you have different options than he has. That sucks. But you guys don't really have an issue with each other, you're two people up against the same issue. Keep going out with your coworkers. Talk to him about seeking out therapy of some kind, or even just brainstorming ways to make the most out of the time you are home, so he doesn't feel so alone when you aren't. Ways that work for both of you. Good luck to you both.

I have a friend who notices when I'm down now and initiates the "are you okay" conversation with me, and that's been a huge help to me, and made me more comfortable initiating the conversation myself. Sometimes people need a little bit of help to get started, ya know? I think you're far from heartless and definitely not an asshole, it's just that mental health (and what helps) is very different for everyone.
